items.summary: US Treasury chief says Iran airlines to be 'shut down' 23 September US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Monday that Iranian airlines will struggle to operate globally in two days under the weight of American sanctions, as the Trump administration intensifies pressure on Tehran. On 23 September, "all the Iranian airlines will be shut down around the world," Bessent told CNBC in an interview as the war launched by the US and Israel nears the seven-month mark. "If they land, you cannot provide them with fuel, you cannot provide them with landing services, you cannot sell them tickets or you will be knocked out of the dollar system," he added. The move follows earlier US sanctions on Iran's aviation industry and Bessent's "economic D-Day" threat on Iran and pledge to choke off Tehran financially.

items.title: Amnesty accuses Iran of crimes against humanity
items.summary: Amnesty International has accused Iranian authorities of committing crimes against humanity during the 2022 Woman, Life, Freedom crackdown, saying more than 500 people, including 71 children, were killed and that the violence disproportionately targeted Kurdish and Baluchi communities. The rights group is urging the UN General Assembly to create an international justice mechanism, arguing that many of the officials it identified remain in positions of power.

items.title: Amnesty says Iran committed 'crimes against humanity' in protests crackdown
items.summary: Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity in the crackdown on 2022 protests that left hundreds dead, Amnesty International said Wednesday, adding Tehran's suppression of new demonstrations this year bore the "same hallmarks" but on an even wider scale. FRANCE 24's Mark Owen speaks with Amnesty International Iran Researcher Raha Bahreini. She calls for the establishment of an international criminal justice mechanism to prosecute those responsible for the crimes.

In a new, more than 1,000-page report titled Architects of Atrocities: State Machinery Orchestrating Crimes Against Humanity in Iran’s 2022 Woman Life Freedom Uprising , the rights group documented the extent of state repression against anti-government protesters during the demonstrations. items.summary: Saudi Arabia says it intercepted Houthi drone near Mecca Saudi Arabia's air defences intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone south of Mecca on Tuesday before it entered prohibited airspace over the holy city, said a spokesman for the Saudi-led military coalition fighting Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis. The security of Islam's two holiest sites and of pilgrims was a "red line", coalition spokesperson Turki al-Malki said early on Wednesday, adding that the coalition would take necessary deterrent measures against the Houthis. Mecca, home to shrines sacred to Muslims worldwide, is Islam's holiest city and the focal point of the annual hajj pilgrimage, one of the five pillars of Islam, which millions of Muslims undertake each year. Malki described the incident as the second Houthi attempt to target Mecca, following what the coalition said was a ballistic missile launch in July 2017. The US Defense Department’s inspector general released the first report on the war with Iran, covering 1 April through 30 June. According to the Pentagon watchdog, munitions expenditure during the war "has resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply". To mitigate the constraints, the report said that the Pentagon is "working to streamline procurement processes and production lead times and to stockpile critical materials, components and selected munitions to respond rapidly to a contingency". US President Donald Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth have repeatedly denied media reports over depleted arms stockpiles. items.title: Houthi advance on Aden supply route repelled, say Saudi-backed forces
items.summary: Houthi advance on Aden supply route repelled, say Saudi-backed forces Yemen's Saudi-backed forces said on Thursday that they had repelled overnight attacks by the Houthis on a key supply route to the southern port city of Aden, where the government is based. The mountain pass known as Hejat al-Abd is a lifeline for forces fighting on behalf of Yemen's Saudi-backed government, which has been hemmed in by a lightning Houthi advance this month linked to the war on Iran. The road is also critical for goods entering Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, and its southern and western rural areas, Reuters reported. It is the only route for residents seeking to travel abroad, with no commercial flights operating from Houthi-controlled areas. The Iran-aligned Houthis have kept up pressure on government forces as they seek to consolidate gains made nearly two weeks ago, when their offensive along Yemen's western coast brought them to the shores of the Red Sea's strategic Bab al-Mandab strait, through which at least ten percent of global maritime trade usually passes.

items.summary: Oil prices fall after Trump hails 'very productive' US-Iran talks at UN Oil prices fell on Wednesday after President Donald Trump said US and Iranian representatives had met for "very good" talks at the United Nations. The international benchmark, Brent crude, and main US contract, West Texas Intermediate, dipped to $98.91 and $89.93 per barrel respectively in early Asian trade -- well below the symbolic $100 mark they have smashed repeatedly since the Middle Eat war broke out in February. The three-hour meeting was "very good", "very productive" and "they have another one scheduled in the very near future", Trump told reporters as he met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Trump's announcement came just hours after he delivered a bellicose address to the UN in which he said he faced a "big decision" on whether to make a deal with Iran or "annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly". Report by AFP

items.summary: Pakistan interior minister heads to Tehran amid regional tensions Pakistan's interior minister Syed Mohsin Naqvi left Islamabad for Tehran on Monday for talks with Iranian officials, according to Mehr News Agency. The report said that Naqvi's visit will focus on expanding bilateral relations and coordination on matters of mutual interest. Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said on Saturday the visit would mainly follow up on previous understandings between the two countries, especially decisions made at the leadership level. Pakistan, which has played a mediating role between Iran and the United States, could also raise regional issues during the visit, Baghaei said, but there was no indication Naqvi was carrying a specific message or proposal from Washington. Naqvi has travelled to Tehran several times since Pakistan began its mediation efforts between the two countries.

items.title: US refuses visas for Iran UN delegation members
items.summary: US refuses visas for Iran UN delegation members The United States has refused to issue visas to members of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian's delegation, including his communications team, for this week's trip to the UN General Assembly, Iranian state media reported Monday. Pezeshkian will be the highest-ranking Iranian official to enter the US since the war began, with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in February. "In an unprecedented hostile move by the US government, (US President Donald) Trump has denied US visas to certain members of the president's high-level delegation, including members of his communications team," state news agency IRNA reported. The Mehr news agency also carried the story, citing a spokesperson for the Iranian presidency, and added that Pezeshkian would address the UN General Assembly on Wednesday.

items.title: Iran says it conveyed conditions to re-engage in talks, end war with US
items.summary: Iran says it conveyed conditions to re-engage in talks, end war with US Iran has conveyed its conditions to mediators for re-engaging in negotiations aimed at ending the war with the US, Iran's Security Chief Mohsen Rezaei said on Saturday in an interview with Al Jazeera. The conditions, which include ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian funds and ending the naval blockade, had been communicated to the US via mediator Qatar, Rezaei stated, adding that a response from President Trump is awaited. Iran has become convinced of the need to change its strategy toward Washington following the US withdrawal from the memorandum of understanding, Rezaei stated. He said Iran knows the US military’s vulnerabilities and is more prepared than ever to counter its air strikes, adding that it recently tested an anti-ship missile near a US aircraft carrier. The security chief also said Iran seeks an end to the war between Saudi Arabia and Yemen's Houthis. He believes the Houthis, too, seek an agreement with Saudi Arabia.

Macron said the meeting would focus on coordinating strategic stockpile levels, cooperation on exports and production capacity, and possible releases of strategic reserves. Macron said that the aim of the meeting was to strengthen cooperation and avoid unnecessary tensions between G7 countries and their key partners. He said France had initiated an international defence mission with the International Maritime Organization last April aimed at escorting tankers and container ships through the strategic waterway once an agreement was reached. Macron said reopening Hormuz depended on a deal between Iran and the United States, which he said appeared unlikely in the short term. The comments came as France faces growing pressure over sharply higher fuel

items.title: Pakistan ready to implement Mecca pact with Saudi Arabia and Turkey, defence minister says
items.summary: Pakistan ready to implement Mecca pact with Saudi Arabia and Turkey, defence minister says Pakistan has said it is ready to implement its defence agreement with Saudi Arabia and Turkey, amid recent Houthi attacks. Pakistan’s Defence Minister Khawaja Asif said in an interview with Pakistani TV channel Geo News that the Mecca agreement - a defence deal between Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey - "applies to us and we will fulfil our duty". He affirmed that Islamabad remains committed to protecting Saudi Arabia and its holy sites. Asif added that there was "absolutely no ambiguity" about the implementation of the defence pact, but did not disclose any further details about its defence strategy. He further said that Pakistan had conveyed Saudi Arabia's message to Iran over the Houthi attacks, and insisted that Iran would not "open another front".

items.title: Report: Hormuz traffic on Tuesday below 10-day average
items.summary: Report: Hormuz traffic on Tuesday below 10-day average Three commodity vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, down from four a day earlier and below the 10-day moving average of about 15, preliminary shipping data showed on Wednesday. The figures may change as some ships typically switch off their transponders during the voyage. All three vessels, including one Panamax tanker, were exiting the strait, the data from shiptracker Kpler showed at 0200 GMT. One ballast liquefied natural gas tanker, Al Mafyar, however reappeared inside the strait on Tuesday, after being last seen outside of the waterway on September 19, according to both Kpler and LSEG data. The Strait of Hormuz carried a fifth of the world's oil and gas before the US-Iran conflict. Meanwhile, 22 commodity vessels transited the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on Tuesday, another maritime chokepoint on the southwest tip of Yemen and a vital trade route for oil between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. Their remarks came as Republican candidates in some of the tightest election races in November called for the measure as a way to curb record fuel prices. Diesel prices have shot to record highs in the US and Europe as wars in Iran and Ukraine sharply cut exports from some of the biggest producers such as Russia, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. "I've said let's not send out the diesel. We make a lot of diesel ... I've called for it. Few have profited from this privatization of the U.S. military more than the CEOs of Pentagon contractors. items.title: President Iran toont bij VN foto's van oorlogsslachtoffers, delegatie VS vertrekt
items.summary: In zijn toespraak op de Algemene Vergadering van de Verenigde Naties in New York heeft de Iraanse president Pezeshkian gezegd dat de inwoners van zijn land de afgelopen zeven maanden "slachtoffer van terrorisme" zijn geweest. "We hebben onszelf alleen maar verdedigd", aldus Pezeshkian, "wij zijn geen terroristen". De toespraak van Pezeshkian was een dag na die van de Amerikaanse president Trump. Die zei dat hij de islamitische republiek mogelijk zal "vernietigen" als er niet snel een akkoord wordt gesloten over de beëindiging van de oorlog tussen de VS en Iran. Donald Trump used his address to the general assembly to threaten Iran , another member state, with annihilation again. The charter also speaks of the obligations of international law. On Venezuela, Mr Trump gloated that “to the victor belong the spoils”. His speech in New York on Tuesday might be regarded as an improvement on last year’s only in that it was not an explicit, full-scale attack on the UN itself, merely on its founding principles. items.summary: For years, Saudi Arabia's security posture rested on a quiet assumption: that Washington would show up when it mattered. items.summary: The Bunker appears originally at the Project on Government Oversight and is republished here with permission. You shouldn’t go to war without the backing of the U.S. Congress. President Donald Trump is learning that the hard way, as his — not our — six-month-and-counting “ little excursion ” and “ small potatoes ” Iranian quagmire drags on. And you don’t build weapons for tomorrow’s wars — especially the ones you say are critical to future victories (remember them?) — using the parliamentary peek-a-boo prestidigitation known as reconciliation . In both instances, Trump is seeking big changes in U.S. national security as unilaterally as possible, with minimal congressional backing. Reconciliation is a controversial process to fund programs. It doesn’t have to follow the standard congressional appropriation rules. Most critically, reconciliation bills aren’t subject to a Senate filibuster . items.summary: Aan de opmars van de Houthi's in Jemen lijkt voorlopig geen einde te komen. Volgens persbureau Reuters proberen de door Iran gesteunde strijders nu ook het strategisch gelegen Kahboub-gebergte in het zuidwesten van Jemen in handen te krijgen. Als dat lukt, wordt de greep van de Houthi's op de Straat van Bab al-Mandab nog steviger. En dat terwijl de Houthi's een maand geleden alleen nog het noordwesten van Jemen onder controle hadden. Sinds juli is het geweld tussen de militante groepering en Saudi-Arabië opgelaaid, en onlangs begonnen de Houthi's een grondoffensief. Daarbij namen ze al de steden Mokka en Dhubab en het eiland Perim in, waarmee het de controle over de belangrijke zeestraat Bab al-Mandab in handen kreeg. Die is belangrijk voor de internationale zeevaart, zeker nu de Straat van Hormuz sinds februari vrijwel afgesloten is vanwege de oorlog tussen de VS en Iran. Daarmee hebben de Houthi's een belangrijke troef in handen. Toch ondervonden ze weinig weerstand bij hun opmars naar de zeestraat. Hoe konden de Houthi's zo snel en ogenschijnlijk makkelijk oprukken? items.summary: Jake and Logan Paul were invited to give a motivational speech. Just don’t let them get involved with military policy We’re now approaching month seven of a war against Iran that Donald Trump repeatedly assured us would be over in a matter of weeks . Prices are rising, troop morale is plummeting , and there is little evidence things will improve. The situation is so desperate that the decision makers at the Pentagon have decided to bring out the big guns. I’m not talking about nuclear weapons, although Trump recently threatened to “blow the entire nation [of Iran] up”. No, I’m talking about influencers Jake and Logan Paul, who are famous for doing idiotic stunts on YouTube and getting hit in the face during boxing matches. Last Thursday, Pete Hegseth’s Department of Defense or whatever they’re calling it these days (the Department of War Crimes ?) welcomed the Paul brothers to Washington DC “to meet with our warriors” and deliver a motivational speech. In response, former Republican congressman and air force officer Adam Kinzinger wrote , “We aren’t a serious country at the moment.”

items.title: Trump still thinks Iranians will ‘rise up’ against the government. In Tehran I see a different story | Hossein Hamdieh
items.summary: If anything, the ongoing war is uniting a divided country against the foreign invaders. Washington seems a long way from grasping this point The US president, Donald Trump, asked recently on one of his Truth Social rants : “When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?” So frenetic and all-over-the-place are Trump’s statements that one does not know which are actual policies and which are simply noise. But if counting on the “Iranian people” to rise up and fight is indeed US policy then, as far as I can tell from within Iran, it is a failed one. And miserably so. At least for now. There is no reliable nationwide polling that can tell us what Iranians think about the war in real time. So this is an observation, not a poll. It comes from conversations I have had with many people. Hossein Hamdieh holds a joint PhD in Geography and Anthropology from Humboldt University of Berlin and King’s College London. items.summary: Washington talks about “influence” as though it were a mystical vapor that leaks out of every military base closure. But Beijing’s rapidly growing clout in the Middle East shows that influence can come in many forms. While the Pentagon debates whether and where to rebuild U.S. bases battered by Iran during Operation Epic Fury, China has spent the last decade expanding its influence in the Middle East without stationing a single soldier there. clusters.headline: When Saudi Arabia realizes it's backed the wrong horse

items.summary: The United States went to war with Iran in the belief that American power could quickly overwhelm Tehran’s ability to threaten the Middle East. For Saudi Arabia, the war is producing nearly the opposite result. Iran has been badly hit, but it and its regional allies have demonstrated that they can still threaten Saudi cities, oil installations, pipelines and export routes. At the same time, Washington has shown that even overwhelming offensive power does not necessarily translate into effective protection for its Gulf partners. The consequence is likely to be a historic Saudi reassessment: less confidence in the United States, more reliance on regional partners and a much closer strategic relationship with China. clusters.headline: UK's Burnham agrees to Saudi request for refuelling support

items.title: UK's Burnham agrees to Saudi request for refuelling support
items.summary: UK's Burnham agrees to Saudi request for refuelling support British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday he had agreed to a request from Saudi Arabia to provide defensive air-to-air refuelling for a limited time, a move he described as helping to stabilise the wider region. Riyadh requested support after the Houthis, who control the most populous parts of Yemen, intensified their attacks on Saudi Arabia, a new front in the wider war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February. "We have received a request from the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia for military support, and on the advice of the defence secretary and the foreign secretary, last night I agreed to that request for defensive air-to-air refuelling," he told reporters as he travelled to New York for a meeting of the United Nations General Assembly. "Because of course Saudi Arabia has been experiencing attack... and we need to keep those pathways open, and hence our agreement to the request," he said.

De groep dreigde vorige week al pijpleidingen van een aantal olievelden af te sluiten als hun eisen niet werden ingewilligd. items.title: Midterm elections: Trump looms large over 2026 vote as Democrats eye gains
items.summary: With the US midterm elections now just six weeks away, we’ll speak to our Washington correspondent Fraser Jackson about whether President Donald Trump could help or hurt his party’s chances. Polls have pointed to what some are calling a “blue wave”, with Democrats potentially regaining control of the House, while the Senate race remains more uncertain. Trump has ramped up campaigning, including spending heavily on advertising and proposing $5,000 payments to voters who support Republicans. But with his approval ratings under pressure amid the war in Iran and the Middle East, and rising oil, gasoline and commodity prices compared with before he took office, the political landscape could still shift significantly in the coming weeks.

Mohebbi said US forces had been forced to relocate troops and equipment from regional bases to more distant positions, but US intelligence centres remained within Iran’s reach and that the, Press TV reported. Mohebbi also said that US technological superiority had failed to overcome Iran’s defensive and offensive capabilities. He warned that Iran still had targets linked to US interests that had not yet been struck, saying the IRGC remained prepared to respond to any further escalation.

items.summary: Inlichtingendiensten AIVD en MIVD gebruiken in toenemende mate AI en andere algoritmes, maar er zijn te weinig waarborgen om de risico's in te dammen. De inlichtingendiensten gebruiken zowel kunstmatige intelligentie als geautomatiseerde data-analyse (GDA) om gegevens te verwerken, teksten samen te vatten of vertalingen uit te voeren, schrijft de toezichthouder. Een centraal overzicht of een AI-beleid was er tijdens het onderzoek van de CTIVD niet. Daardoor hangt veel af van het individuele oordeel van de medewerkers die AI-systemen maken. Omdat er geen goed overzicht is van het gebruik van AI, is het ook moeilijk voor de toezichthouder om te beoordelen of de diensten zich aan de regels houden. items.summary: Pakistan's Naqvi arrives in Tehran amid looming fears of renewed US-Iran war Pakistan’s interior minister Mohsin Naqvi arrived in Tehran on Monday, where he was received by his Iranian counterpart Eskandar Momeni, Iran’s Tasnim news agency said. The visit would focus on bilateral ties and reviewing the agreements signed earlier by senior officials of the two countries, Tasnim reported. The visit comes as fears of a renewed US-Iran war are looming amid heightened tensions and the collapse of earlier negotiations. Tensions remain high in the region, but Pakistan and Iran have kept diplomatic contacts and Islamabad has in the past tried to broker dialogue between Tehran and Washington. Since Pakistan began to mediate between Iran and the United States, Naqvi has visited Tehran several times.

items.summary: Trump’s mess has rekindled Yemen’s civil war and a years-long conflict between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia When the US and Israel launched a war of aggression against Iran in late February, Tehran’s allies in the Middle East jumped into the fray. Lebanon’s Hezbollah militia fired rockets at Israel, while Shia militias in Iraq attacked US bases and diplomatic outposts. But the Houthis, who control large parts of Yemen, mostly stayed on the sidelines. Over the past few weeks, however, the Houthis have changed their tactics and have entered the conflict in full force. They led a rapid advance along Yemen’s Red Sea coast, seizing a strategic port city and several islands that gave the militia control over the Bab al-Mandab strait, a vital waterway for energy shipments and other global trade. Thanks to Donald Trump’s war, Iran and its allies now dominate the Middle East’s two major regional energy chokepoints: Bab al-Mandab and the strait of Hormuz. Continue reading...

items.title: Ghalibaf: Iran must ‘fight and negotiate’ as war with US drags on
items.summary: Ghalibaf: Iran must ‘fight and negotiate’ as war with US drags on Iran’s parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on Sunday said that Tehran must fight and negotiate as its near seven-month war with the United States drags on. Addressing the parliament, Ghalibaf said Iran would use its military might to “push the enemy back and deal them devastating blows” at crucial junctures, but would resort to diplomacy when it has the upper hand on the battlefield. The Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until the United States fulfilled its commitments, according to Ghalibaf, who said Iran's negotiating position was “entirely clear, rational, and non-negotiable”. His remarks come after Pakistani and Qatari mediators have reportedly been told that Iran has seven conditions which must be met before talks with Washington can begin.

clusters.headline: Iran says Hormuz will not reopen until US honours June agreement

items.title: Iran says Hormuz will not reopen until US honours June agreement
items.summary: Iran says Hormuz will not reopen until US honours June agreement Iran’s parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said on Sunday that the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed until the United States fulfils its commitments under a June agreement and meets Tehran’s conditions. Speaking in parliament, Ghalibaf said Iran had “explicitly conveyed its conditions to the opposing side through intermediaries”, according to Iran’s state broadcaster IRIB. Reuters has previously reported that Tehran has tied the reopening of the strait to US commitments under the June memorandum, including lifting its blockade of Iranian ports, oil sanctions and other measures. “The enemy is well aware that the path of deception and unilateral imposition is closed,” Ghalibaf said, adding that there would be no return to negotiations or reopening of the waterway until Iran’s rights were recognised and US commitments fulfilled. The Strait of Hormuz is a major route for global oil and gas shipments, and traffic through the waterway has remained sharply below pre-war levels amid the continuing tensions.

clusters.headline: Baghaei says attending UNGA meet Iran's right, not favour granted by US

items.title: Baghaei says attending UNGA meet Iran's right, not favour granted by US
items.summary: Baghaei says attending UNGA meet Iran's right, not favour granted by US Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei has said that Iran will not abandon its right to be present in the UN General Assembly, stressing that attending the UN meeting is not a privilege given by Washington, according to IRNA. Speaking in a televised programme, Baghaei said that being in New York held absolutely no charm for Iranian representatives, but it was a "trench that must not be abandoned". He said participating in the UN General Assembly was a legal right rather than a favour from others, as Iran was one of the 50 founding member states of the UN. Baghaei said that the country had a duty to attend the most important international event to make the rights of the Iranian people heard by the world. He added that the US "used every tool to prevent the Iranian delegation’s participation, ranging from derogatory remarks and media propaganda to abusing its commitments as the host government by creating delays or refusing to issue visas for several delegation members", IRNA reported.

clusters.headline: Turkish foreign minister says Israel should not 'chase empty dreams'

items.title: Turkish foreign minister says Israel should not 'chase empty dreams'
items.summary: Turkish foreign minister says Israel should not 'chase empty dreams' Turkish Parliament Speaker Numan Kurtulmus has accused Israel of seeking to deepen divisions across the Middle East in its pursuit for a 'promised land'. “Israel should not chase empty dreams,” Kurtulmus said during a civil society gathering in Kirsehir, according to Al Jazeera. “Israel’s main goal is for the peoples of this region to fall out with each other, to fight each other, and to realise its own ‘promised land’,” he added. However, he said, Turkey "will bring this region together and continue on our path". Kurtulmus said Israel had carried out attacks in recent years against Palestine, Iran, Iraq, Syria, Lebanon, Yemen and Qatar, arguing that almost every country in the region had been affected by conflict. “They want to divide and fragment; we want to unite and integrate,” Kurtulmus said. “They want to scatter; we want to bring people together.”

items.title: Iran disputes US oil claim, approves new rule on Hormuz data cables
items.summary: Iran disputes US oil claim, approves new rule on Hormuz data cables Iran has disputed a claim by US Central Command (Centcom) that it escorted tankers carrying more than a billion barrels of oil through the Strait of Hormuz. Armed forces spokesman Abolfazl Shekarchi called the claim a “failed psychological operation” meant to boost US troop morale and justify the war’s financial and human costs, Iran’s Fars news agency reported. Centcom had also said it protected more than 2,000 commercial transits through the strait and cleared its main shipping lanes of mines, in addition to facilitating oil exports. Separately, a committee of senior Iranian officials has approved a rule requiring Tehran’s approval for data cables routed through the strait, Fars reported. The measure, known as Article 10, will also apply to other data communications equipment passing through the waterway, with further details to be set out in upcoming regulations.

items.title: Reducing the Risk of Nuclear War: The Long View
items.summary: Matthew Bunn on the factors driving the risk of nuclear war — and how we shift them toward greater safety, for ourselves and for future generations. Location: The Foundry, 101 Rogers St, Cambridge Some of the most consequential decisions our civilization makes — decisions that will shape the lives of countless future generations — concern nuclear weapons and the risk of nuclear war. Harvard's Matthew Bunn will join Long Now Boston to take the long view on one of humanity's defining challenges. A nuclear war is unlikely to come "out of a clear blue sky." It is far more likely to arise from a crisis or conflict between nuclear-armed states that escalates step by step. Bunn offers a structured way of thinking about reducing the risk at each of those steps: lowering the chance of conflict among nuclear-armed states in the first place; keeping any conflict that does occur from crossing the nuclear threshold; and ensuring that, if nuclear weapons are ever used, the exchange does not escalate to hundreds or thousands of weapons. items.title: Araghchi says Middle East needs dialogue, not foreign military presence
items.summary: Araghchi says Middle East needs dialogue, not foreign military presence Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Saturday called for greater reliance on dialogue, cooperation and multilateral institutions. Speaking virtually at Indonesia's Global Town Hall 2026, Araghchi said: "Sustainable security in the Middle East cannot be dictated from outside the region." Araghchi said ignoring international law when it conflicts with the interests of major powers undermines the rule of law, while the failure of international institutions such as the United Nations to respond to aggression and hold violators accountable could damage their credibility. "We believe that sustainable security can be achieved through dialogue, trust-building, cooperation and mutual respect among the countries of the region, not through the military presence of foreign powers and the imposition of their will," he said.

clusters.headline: The Houthis could tip the Iran war in Tehran's favor

items.title: The Houthis could tip the Iran war in Tehran's favor
items.summary: The conflict between the United States and Iran has become a contest in enduring economic pain and the political consequences that may flow from that pain. This has characterized the conflict since the breakdown of the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) in June that had raised brief hopes that the war would end. Each side appears confident that it can outlast the other in the pain-endurance contest. Fundamental change of this situation is unlikely anytime soon despite some indications Iran is considering military escalation as a possible way to break the stalemate. The Trump administration, after the failure of other options, appears to be hoping that the Iranian regime either will be toppled by an economically strained Iranian public or will somehow give up and make concessions. One of the more significant recent developments with potential for changing this stalemate, however, is renewed military action by the Houthi regime in Yemen, which includes interdicting shipping traversing the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb Strait. items.title: Over 150 countries reject US decision to bar Palestinian delegation from upcoming UN General Assembly
items.summary: Over 150 countries reject US decision to bar Palestinian delegation from upcoming UN General Assembly On Thursday, 152 countries voted in favour of a resolution adopted by the UN General Assembly, rejecting the US's decision to prevent the Palestinian delegation from participating in the upcoming UN General Assembly session in New York City. The resolution called on Washington to reverse the decision, considering it a clear violation of the Headquarters Agreement, which legally obliges the host country to facilitate the entry of diplomatic delegations. items.summary: C'est une fable acerbe de l’Iran aujourd’hui, macabre et burlesque, avec un équilibre parfait entre l’humour noir et une critique sociale féroce. Dans le film Living Twice, Dying Thrice (« Deux vies, trois morts »), Karim Lakzadeh, né en 1986 à Chiraz, dans la province du Fars en Iran, raconte l’histoire de trois mineurs qui traversent le pays clandestinement. Victimes de l’effondrement d’une mine, ils décident de se faire déclarer morts pour commencer une deuxième vie. Présenté en première mondiale au Festival de Cannes, le film sera projeté au cinéma Louxor, à Paris, à l’occasion de la reprise de la programmation de l’ACID, du 17 au 20 septembre, dédiée au renouvellement des regards cinématographiques.

Over the last two weeks, that assumption has been tested more severely than at any point since 2015, when Saudi Arabia initially launched its military intervention to roll back Houthi control of the Yemeni capital Sanaa. If losing the Red Sea coast was a blow to the government, losing Marib would be a decisive defeat. While this is significantly lower than the $100-billion-plus price tag independent experts have calculated, CBO notes that its estimates were limited because “DoD did not respond to CBO’s requests for information.” Without help from the DoD, CBO could not include a number of known war costs in its analysis, including repairing damage to U.S. military bases in the region. Those costs alone could top $200 billion , according to experts. What CBO could confirm was that the war has been a disaster for the U.S. economy and military readiness. The CBO analysis estimates that the inflation rate is now expected to be a full half-point higher in 2027 than it was before the war began, almost entirely because of higher global energy costs result

The resolution is quite a brief against Hegseth, covering U.S. military actions in Iran, Yemen, and Venezuela, as well as accusing Hegseth of minimizing civilian deaths and abridging freedom of speech. Impeachment votes are privileged in the House, which means the measure can bypass the rules and go straight to a floor vote after debate. The articles would have to get a motion, however, which would require a majority vote. It is not clear how many Democrats would vote for it. Zo kan het Iraanse regime toegang krijgen tot contactpersonen, e-mails en socialemedia-accounts van het slachtoffer. Gepensioneerden krijgen er geld bij doordat pensioenfondsen er goed voorstaan en daardoor de pensioenen kunnen verhogen. De koopkracht van de laagste inkomens groeit een beetje doordat werkenden een grotere korting krijgen op hun inkomstenbelasting. "Er gebeurt wel iets om voor bepaalde groepen de koopkracht iets op te krikken", zegt CPB-directeur Pieter Hasekamp. "Het kabinet heeft ervoor gekozen om werkenden een steuntje in de rug te geven door die arbeidskorting iets te verhogen." items.summary: Last week, the war in Ukraine reached deep inside the Russian Arctic. On September 9, Ukrainian drones struck two gas processing plants in the Yamalo-Nenets region, located about 1,900 miles from the Ukrainian border. This is Ukraine’s deepest strike on Russia since the war began. Arctic energy infrastructure in the Yamal region produces around 80% of Russia's natural gas. Russian military analysts believe the Ukrainian drones were launched from Sumy, northern Ukraine, and reached all the way into Yamal with the help of Starlink. Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces announced , “Until today, this was considered an absolutely safe rear.” The attack also shook European energy markets, as Europe buys large volumes of gas from the Yamal region. President Donald Trump later told Ukraine to stop attacking Russia’s diesel infrastructure, saying fuel shortages due to the strikes were “hurting the world,” without explicitly acknowledging the fact that the spike in global energy prices is largely driven by the Iran war. items.title: Houthi advance on Aden supply route repelled, say Saudi-backed forces
items.summary: Houthi advance on Aden supply route repelled, say Saudi-backed forces Yemen's Saudi-backed forces said on Thursday that they had repelled overnight attacks by the Houthis on a key supply route to the southern port city of Aden, where the government is based. The mountain pass known as Hejat al-Abd is a lifeline for forces fighting on behalf of Yemen's Saudi-backed government, which has been hemmed in by a lightning Houthi advance this month linked to the war on Iran. The road is also critical for goods entering Taiz, Yemen's third-largest city, and its southern and western rural areas, Reuters reported. It is the only route for residents seeking to travel abroad, with no commercial flights operating from Houthi-controlled areas. The Iran-aligned Houthis have kept up pressure on government forces as they seek to consolidate gains made nearly two weeks ago, when their offensive along Yemen's western coast brought them to the shores of the Red Sea's strategic Bab al-Mandab strait, through which at least ten percent of global maritime trade usually passes.

On Sunday, Germany’s far right won another state election , taking nearly 40% of the vote in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. France is preparing a €54bn fiscal squeeze, which could turn the screw still further on a foundering so-called European social model. At the UN general assembly, Donald Trump once again threatened to “annihilate” Iran, even as the fourth failed western war on a Muslim nation this century has added more than $100bn to Americans’ fuel bills. There is little dispute over the symptoms. The great fight of our age is over the diagnosis, and the right has been winning it for years. Donald Trump used his address to the general assembly to threaten Iran , another member state, with annihilation again. The charter also speaks of the obligations of international law. On Venezuela, Mr Trump gloated that “to the victor belong the spoils”. His speech in New York on Tuesday might be regarded as an improvement on last year’s only in that it was not an explicit, full-scale attack on the UN itself, merely on its founding principles. The absences this year are perhaps as telling as the US president’s hostile presence. Vladimir Putin has not attended for more than a decade. Nor has Xi Jinping – but the snub is more striking as he is in Washington to meet the US president. items.title: Yemen crisis reminds Saudi Arabia of imperative to navigate tough realities
items.summary: For years, Saudi Arabia's security posture rested on a quiet assumption: that Washington would show up when it mattered. The dramatic events in Sept. 2019 tested that assumption directly. Claimed by Yemen’s Ansarullah movement but blamed on Iran, drone and missile strikes on the Abqaiq and Khurais oil facilities knocked out roughly half of Saudi production overnight—one of the most consequential attacks on Gulf Arab energy infrastructure in decades. The United States did not respond militarily. That non-response is now widely read as the moment the assumption broke. items.summary: Report: Hormuz traffic on Tuesday below 10-day average Three commodity vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday, down from four a day earlier and below the 10-day moving average of about 15, preliminary shipping data showed on Wednesday. The figures may change as some ships typically switch off their transponders during the voyage. All three vessels, including one Panamax tanker, were exiting the strait, the data from shiptracker Kpler showed at 0200 GMT. One ballast liquefied natural gas tanker, Al Mafyar, however reappeared inside the strait on Tuesday, after being last seen outside of the waterway on September 19, according to both Kpler and LSEG data. The Strait of Hormuz carried a fifth of the world's oil and gas before the US-Iran conflict. Meanwhile, 22 commodity vessels transited the Bab el-Mandeb Strait on Tuesday, another maritime chokepoint on the southwest tip of Yemen and a vital trade route for oil between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. items.title: Trump still thinks Iranians will ‘rise up’ against the government. In Tehran I see a different story | Hossein Hamdieh
items.summary: If anything, the ongoing war is uniting a divided country against the foreign invaders. Washington seems a long way from grasping this point The US president, Donald Trump, asked recently on one of his Truth Social rants : “When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?” So frenetic and all-over-the-place are Trump’s statements that one does not know which are actual policies and which are simply noise. But if counting on the “Iranian people” to rise up and fight is indeed US policy then, as far as I can tell from within Iran, it is a failed one. And miserably so. At least for now. There is no reliable nationwide polling that can tell us what Iranians think about the war in real time. So this is an observation, not a poll. It comes from conversations I have had with many people. Hossein Hamdieh holds a joint PhD in Geography and Anthropology from Humboldt University of Berlin and King’s College London. items.title: China is outfoxing the US in the battle for Mideast influence
items.summary: Washington talks about “influence” as though it were a mystical vapor that leaks out of every military base closure. But Beijing’s rapidly growing clout in the Middle East shows that influence can come in many forms. While the Pentagon debates whether and where to rebuild U.S. bases battered by Iran during Operation Epic Fury, China has spent the last decade expanding its influence in the Middle East without stationing a single soldier there. China’s experience in the region makes clear that influence can be cultivated far more cheaply than Washington assumes, and without maintaining a sprawling network of vulnerable military installations. As Operation Epic Fury demonstrated, Washington’s constellation of fixed bases across the Middle East is vulnerable and expensive to defend. Before the war, the United States maintained at least 19 military facilities across the region, eight of them considered permanent. items.title: When Saudi Arabia realizes it's backed the wrong horse
items.summary: The United States went to war with Iran in the belief that American power could quickly overwhelm Tehran’s ability to threaten the Middle East. For Saudi Arabia, the war is producing nearly the opposite result. Iran has been badly hit, but it and its regional allies have demonstrated that they can still threaten Saudi cities, oil installations, pipelines and export routes. At the same time, Washington has shown that even overwhelming offensive power does not necessarily translate into effective protection for its Gulf partners. The consequence is likely to be a historic Saudi reassessment: less confidence in the United States, more reliance on regional partners and a much closer strategic relationship with China. Saudi Arabia’s geographical problem is not new. In an article published in LobeLog in September 2019 , I described the “encirclement” of Saudi oil production by Iran and Iran-aligned forces. items.summary: UK's Burnham agrees to Saudi request for refuelling support British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday he had agreed to a request from Saudi Arabia to provide defensive air-to-air refuelling for a limited time, a move he described as helping to stabilise the wider region. Riyadh requested support after the Houthis, who control the most populous parts of Yemen, intensified their attacks on Saudi Arabia, a new front in the wider war that began with US and Israeli strikes on Iran in late February. "We have received a request from the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia for military support, and on the advice of the defence secretary and the foreign secretary, last night I agreed to that request for defensive air-to-air refuelling," he told reporters as he travelled to New York for a meeting of the United Nations General Assembly. "Because of course Saudi Arabia has been experiencing attack... and we need to keep those pathways open, and hence our agreement to the request," he said.

De groep dreigde vorige week al pijpleidingen van een aantal olievelden af te sluiten als hun eisen niet werden ingewilligd. De groep wil dat hun organisatie "financieel en administratief" onder de NOC wordt gebracht. De groep valt nu onder het Libische ministerie van Defensie. On 23 September, "all the Iranian airlines will be shut down around the world," Bessent told CNBC in an interview as the war launched by the US and Israel nears the seven-month mark. "If they land, you cannot provide them with fuel, you cannot provide them with landing services, you cannot sell them tickets or you will be knocked out of the dollar system," he added. items.title: Ghalibaf: Iran must ‘fight and negotiate’ as war with US drags on
items.summary: Ghalibaf: Iran must ‘fight and negotiate’ as war with US drags on Iran’s parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf on Sunday said that Tehran must fight and negotiate as its near seven-month war with the United States drags on. Addressing the parliament, Ghalibaf said Iran would use its military might to “push the enemy back and deal them devastating blows” at crucial junctures, but would resort to diplomacy when it has the upper hand on the battlefield. The Strait of Hormuz would remain closed until the United States fulfilled its commitments, according to Ghalibaf, who said Iran's negotiating position was “entirely clear, rational, and non-negotiable”. His remarks come after Pakistani and Qatari mediators have reportedly been told that Iran has seven conditions which must be met before talks with Washington can begin.

items.title: Iran says Hormuz will not reopen until US honours June agreement
items.summary: Iran says Hormuz will not reopen until US honours June agreement Iran’s parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said on Sunday that the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed until the United States fulfils its commitments under a June agreement and meets Tehran’s conditions. Speaking in parliament, Ghalibaf said Iran had “explicitly conveyed its conditions to the opposing side through intermediaries”, according to Iran’s state broadcaster IRIB. Reuters has previously reported that Tehran has tied the reopening of the strait to US commitments under the June memorandum, including lifting its blockade of Iranian ports, oil sanctions and other measures. “The enemy is well aware that the path of deception and unilateral imposition is closed,” Ghalibaf said, adding that there would be no return to negotiations or reopening of the waterway until Iran’s rights were recognised and US commitments fulfilled. The Strait of Hormuz is a major route for global oil and gas shipments, and traffic through the waterway has remained sharply below pre-war levels amid the continuing tensions.

items.title: Baghaei says attending UNGA meet Iran's right, not favour granted by US
items.summary: Baghaei says attending UNGA meet Iran's right, not favour granted by US Iran's foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei has said that Iran will not abandon its right to be present in the UN General Assembly, stressing that attending the UN meeting is not a privilege given by Washington, according to IRNA. Speaking in a televised programme, Baghaei said that being in New York held absolutely no charm for Iranian representatives, but it was a "trench that must not be abandoned". He said participating in the UN General Assembly was a legal right rather than a favour from others, as Iran was one of the 50 founding member states of the UN. Baghaei said that the country had a duty to attend the most important international event to make the rights of the Iranian people heard by the world. He added that the US "used every tool to prevent the Iranian delegation’s participation, ranging from derogatory remarks and media propaganda to abusing its commitments as the host government by creating delays or refusing to issue visas for several delegation members", IRNA reported.

items.title: 'Middle East situation could escalate rapidly': US urges citizens to exercise caution
items.summary: 'Middle East situation could escalate rapidly': US urges citizens to exercise caution The US government has told its citizens currently in the Middle East that the security environment remains "complex with the potential for unforeseen escalation", urging them to  exercise heightened vigilance. Centcom had also said it protected more than 2,000 commercial transits through the strait and cleared its main shipping lanes of mines, in addition to facilitating oil exports. Separately, a committee of senior Iranian officials has approved a rule requiring Tehran’s approval for data cables routed through the strait, Fars reported. The measure, known as Article 10, will also apply to other data communications equipment passing through the waterway, with further details to be set out in upcoming regulations.

items.summary: Matthew Bunn on the factors driving the risk of nuclear war — and how we shift them toward greater safety, for ourselves and for future generations. Location: The Foundry, 101 Rogers St, Cambridge Some of the most consequential decisions our civilization makes — decisions that will shape the lives of countless future generations — concern nuclear weapons and the risk of nuclear war. Harvard's Matthew Bunn will join Long Now Boston to take the long view on one of humanity's defining challenges. A nuclear war is unlikely to come "out of a clear blue sky." It is far more likely to arise from a crisis or conflict between nuclear-armed states that escalates step by step. Bunn offers a structured way of thinking about reducing the risk at each of those steps: lowering the chance of conflict among nuclear-armed states in the first place; keeping any conflict that does occur from crossing the nuclear threshold; and ensuring that, if nuclear weapons are ever used, the exchange does not escalate to hundreds or thousands of weapons. items.title: Araghchi says Middle East needs dialogue, not foreign military presence
items.summary: Araghchi says Middle East needs dialogue, not foreign military presence Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Saturday called for greater reliance on dialogue, cooperation and multilateral institutions. Speaking virtually at Indonesia's Global Town Hall 2026, Araghchi said: "Sustainable security in the Middle East cannot be dictated from outside the region." Araghchi said ignoring international law when it conflicts with the interests of major powers undermines the rule of law, while the failure of international institutions such as the United Nations to respond to aggression and hold violators accountable could damage their credibility. "We believe that sustainable security can be achieved through dialogue, trust-building, cooperation and mutual respect among the countries of the region, not through the military presence of foreign powers and the imposition of their will," he said.

items.title: Macron to convene G7 over energy crisis, says France working to reopen Hormuz
items.summary: Macron to convene G7 over energy crisis, says France working to reopen Hormuz French President Emmanuel Macron has said that he would convene a G7 meeting in the coming weeks to coordinate responses to the energy crisis caused by the Iran war, while reiterating France was working to facilitate the peaceful reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. items.title: Prix du carburant: «Les véritables tensions sont sur le marché du raffinage»

En Syrie, en France, aux États-Unis ou au Guatemala, où les chauffeurs de taxi et les travailleurs des transports se sont mobilisés en bloquant quatre points de la capitale et certains axes de l'intérieur du pays. Après le blocage iranien du détroit d'Ormuz, par où transite habituellement 20 % du commerce mondial d'hydrocarbures, un nouveau front s'est ouvert la semaine passée dans le détroit de Bab-el-Mandeb, après que les houthistes pro-iraniens en ont pris le contrôle. items.title: The Houthis could tip the Iran war in Tehran's favor
items.summary: The conflict between the United States and Iran has become a contest in enduring economic pain and the political consequences that may flow from that pain. This has characterized the conflict since the breakdown of the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) in June that had raised brief hopes that the war would end. Each side appears confident that it can outlast the other in the pain-endurance contest. Fundamental change of this situation is unlikely anytime soon despite some indications Iran is considering military escalation as a possible way to break the stalemate. The Trump administration, after the failure of other options, appears to be hoping that the Iranian regime either will be toppled by an economically strained Iranian public or will somehow give up and make concessions. One of the more significant recent developments with potential for changing this stalemate, however, is renewed military action by the Houthi regime in Yemen, which includes interdicting shipping traversing the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb Strait. items.title: Over 150 countries reject US decision to bar Palestinian delegation from upcoming UN General Assembly
items.summary: Over 150 countries reject US decision to bar Palestinian delegation from upcoming UN General Assembly On Thursday, 152 countries voted in favour of a resolution adopted by the UN General Assembly, rejecting the US's decision to prevent the Palestinian delegation from participating in the upcoming UN General Assembly session in New York City. The resolution called on Washington to reverse the decision, considering it a clear violation of the Headquarters Agreement, which legally obliges the host country to facilitate the entry of diplomatic delegations. The US State Department said on Thursday it has greenlit visas for a core Iranian delegation and essential staffers to take part in the meeting, but denied Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas and other Palestinian officials visas.

US spokesperson Anna Kelly said the UN’s Human Rights Council has “accomplished nothing for human rights while spouting unserious nonsense for decades”, according to remarks carried by The Washington Post on Thursday. “The only party in this conflict that has committed war crimes is the Iranian regime,” Kelly added.

items.title: «Les deux vies et trois morts» du réalisateur iranien Karim Lakzadeh
items.summary: C'est une fable acerbe de l’Iran aujourd’hui, macabre et burlesque, avec un équilibre parfait entre l’humour noir et une critique sociale féroce. Dans le film Living Twice, Dying Thrice (« Deux vies, trois morts »), Karim Lakzadeh, né en 1986 à Chiraz, dans la province du Fars en Iran, raconte l’histoire de trois mineurs qui traversent le pays clandestinement. Victimes de l’effondrement d’une mine, ils décident de se faire déclarer morts pour commencer une deuxième vie. Présenté en première mondiale au Festival de Cannes, le film sera projeté au cinéma Louxor, à Paris, à l’occasion de la reprise de la programmation de l’ACID, du 17 au 20 septembre, dédiée au renouvellement des regards cinématographiques.

items.title: The Guardian view on the Houthi advance in Yemen: another vital Middle East artery becomes a battlefield | Editorial
items.summary: The extraordinary success of the rebels, and Saudi counterstrikes, threaten economic havoc. But the country’s civilians are paying the highest price Even in a region beset by turmoil and learning to expect the unexpected, the lightning advance of Yemen’s Houthis along the Red Sea coast has shocked observers. More than 100,000 people have been forced to flee in a country where immiseration and displacement have become routine and half the population depend on humanitarian aid. But outsiders are paying close attention, because by claiming thousands of kilometres in a matter of days, and seizing strategically important islands, the Iran-backed rebels now control the Bab al-Mandab strait – the other major regional energy chokepoint after the Hormuz strait. The Iran war has forced Saudi Arabia to rely on moving oil via its east-west pipeline to Red Sea ports. Now drone strikes – blamed on an Iran-backed militia in Iraq – have shut the pipeline: on one estimate , a month-long closure could cut global crude supply by 120m barrels. Malki described the incident as the second Houthi attempt to target Mecca, following what the coalition said was a ballistic missile launch in July 2017. items.summary: In the last two days, a pair of government reports confirmed what many outside analysts have claimed: the Iran war has been extraordinarily costly for the U.S. military and for the American public. A Congressional Budget Office (CBO) analysis released Tuesday afternoon found that the Iran war has already cost the Department of Defense (DoD) $38 billion. While this is significantly lower than the $100-billion-plus price tag independent experts have calculated, CBO notes that its estimates were limited because “DoD did not respond to CBO’s requests for information.” Without help from the DoD, CBO could not include a number of known war costs in its analysis, including repairing damage to U.S. military bases in the region. Those costs alone could top $200 billion , according to experts. What CBO could confirm was that the war has been a disaster for the U.S. economy and military readiness. The CBO analysis estimates that the inflation rate is now expected to be a full half-point higher in 2027 than it was before the war began, almost entirely because of higher global energy costs result

items.title: Massie tells RS why he went after Hegseth and not Trump
items.summary: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) tells Responsible Statecraft that he is initiating eight articles of impeachment against Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth because Congress has “exhausted every other remedy to make things right.” After a speech on the floor Tuesday, Massie said is forcing a vote on the articles in the House, which would likely happen on Thursday before the chamber recesses for the midterms. The resolution is quite a brief against Hegseth, covering U.S. military actions in Iran, Yemen, and Venezuela, as well as accusing Hegseth of minimizing civilian deaths and abridging freedom of speech. Impeachment votes are privileged in the House, which means the measure can bypass the rules and go straight to a floor vote after debate. The articles would have to get a motion, however, which would require a majority vote. It is not clear how many Democrats would vote for it. Democrats just killed a resolution to impeach President Donald Trump by one of their own , Rep. Al Green (D-Texas). We spoke to Massie on Tuesday. items.title: Iran war cost US $38bn and significantly depleted missile stockpile, report finds
items.summary: Damaging budget report estimates cost would grow $3bn per month and stockpile could take five years to rebuild The war in Iran has cost the US at least $38bn and left its stockpile of defensive missiles so depleted it could take five years to rebuild, the non-partisan Congressional Budget Office (CBO) has found, in a damaging report less than two months before midterm elections where the war and the cost of living crisis will likely hurt Republicans at the polls. The economic report comes one day after the Pentagon’s inspector general finally released its own first review of the war, saying that the US spent $22.3bn on munitions alone through 30 June, put total spending at $33.4bn and found the fighting had “resulted in strategic inventory shortfalls and revealed industrial base bottlenecks for munitions resupply”. items.title: Iran war cost hits $38bn, forecast to rise $3bn a month, CBO says
items.summary: Iran war cost hits $38bn, forecast to rise $3bn a month, CBO says The six-month-old US war on Iran has cost $38bn so far, and that amount is projected to rise by $3bn a month, Congress's nonpartisan bookkeeper reported on Tuesday, as the Trump administration searches for ways to end the war and reopen the vital Strait of Hormuz. The war is expected to increase inflation by 0.5 percent in the first three months of 2027, according to the Congressional Budget Office accounting, which totalled expenses through 1 August. The mounting costs have strained US munitions stockpiles and driven up energy prices, adding pressure on an already stretched federal budget.

items.title: Iraq eyes Europe as it seeks to diversify oil exports
items.summary: Iraq eyes Europe as it seeks to diversify oil exports Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said on Tuesday that he discussed selling oil to Europe during visits to France and Germany, as Baghdad seeks to diversify its export routes and reduce its reliance on the Strait of Hormuz. During a press conference with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in Berlin, Zaidi said "we want to expand and diversify our export routes". He added that "Iraq cannot remain hostage to a single corridor" as recent events have demonstrated, referring to the Strait of Hormuz, which has been blockaded by Iran during the war. Zaidi said that he had discussed oil exports to Europe with Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron, whom he met in Paris on Monday.

items.title: AIVD: Iran breekt online in bij dissidenten om gevoelige informatie te stelen
items.summary: Iran gebruikt spionagesoftware om gevoelige informatie te verzamelen over kritische Iraniërs die in het Westen wonen. Daarvoor waarschuwt de Nederlandse inlichtingendienst AIVD, samen met de Amerikaanse FBI en het Britse cybersecuritycentrum NCSC. Iraanse diensten proberen via sociale media contact te leggen met dissidenten, activisten en journalisten en hun vertrouwen te winnen. Daarna vragen de Iraanse "cyberactoren" hen om een bestand te downloaden en dat te openen, zeggen de diensten. 'Volledige controle' Zodra het bestand is geopend heeft de software, Chosen Brick, volgens de AIVD "volledige controle over het apparaat". Zo kan het Iraanse regime toegang krijgen tot contactpersonen, e-mails en socialemedia-accounts van het slachtoffer. Ook kan de software beveiligingsinstellingen aanpassen of die in- of uitschakelen en schermafbeeldingen maken. Vooral apparaten van Windows zouden het doelwit zijn. items.summary: De koopkracht ontwikkelt zich volgend jaar iets beter dan in augustus nog geraamd werd. Dat zegt het Centraal Planbureau. In augustus ging het CPB ervan uit dat een doorsnee huishouden er volgend jaar 0,3 procent op achteruitgaat in koopkracht. Door de maatregelen die op Prinsjesdag zijn aangekondigd is de raming nu een achteruitgang van 0,1 procent voor het doorsnee huishouden. Plusje voor laagste inkomens Alleen de laagste inkomens gaan er volgend jaar iets op vooruit: +0,2 procent. En gepensioneerden: +0,3 procent. Gepensioneerden krijgen er geld bij doordat pensioenfondsen er goed voorstaan en daardoor de pensioenen kunnen verhogen. De koopkracht van de laagste inkomens groeit een beetje doordat werkenden een grotere korting krijgen op hun inkomstenbelasting. "Er gebeurt wel iets om voor bepaalde groepen de koopkracht iets op te krikken", zegt CPB-directeur Pieter Hasekamp. "Het kabinet heeft ervoor gekozen om werkenden een steuntje in de rug te geven door die arbeidskorting iets te verhogen." items.title: Ukraine war spreads to Arctic as nuclear tensions escalate
items.summary: Last week, the war in Ukraine reached deep inside the Russian Arctic. On September 9, Ukrainian drones struck two gas processing plants in the Yamalo-Nenets region, located about 1,900 miles from the Ukrainian border. This is Ukraine’s deepest strike on Russia since the war began. Arctic energy infrastructure in the Yamal region produces around 80% of Russia's natural gas. Russian military analysts believe the Ukrainian drones were launched from Sumy, northern Ukraine, and reached all the way into Yamal with the help of Starlink. Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces announced , “Until today, this was considered an absolutely safe rear.” The attack also shook European energy markets, as Europe buys large volumes of gas from the Yamal region. President Donald Trump later told Ukraine to stop attacking Russia’s diesel infrastructure, saying fuel shortages due to the strikes were “hurting the world,” without explicitly acknowledging the fact that the spike in global energy prices is largely driven by the Iran war.
